title: Purpose and result clauses

objectives.can: Tell a purpose clause from a result clause and translate ut and ne accordingly.

explanation.summary: Latin uses *ut* with the subjunctive for two different ideas: the aim of an action (purpose) and its outcome (result). The signal words, the negative and the sense of the sentence decide which one you are reading, and the English translation follows from that decision.

sections.heading: One word, two jobs
body: A purpose clause says what someone did something for: the aim they had in mind. A result clause says what actually followed. Both are subordinate clauses introduced by *ut*, both have a verb in the subjunctive, and in English both can be rendered 'so that'. The difference lies in the meaning, and Latin gives you clues to it.

Luke 5:7 has one of each in a single verse. The fishermen signalled to their partners *ut venirent, et adjuvarent eos*: they did that for a reason, to bring help. The verse goes on with *ita ut pene mergerentur*: the boats were filled with the result that they very nearly sank. Nobody wanted that; it is what happened. The first clause is purpose, the second is result.

sections.heading: Purpose: ut and ne
body: A purpose clause has *ut* with the subjunctive when the aim is positive, and *ne* when it is negative ('so that not', 'lest'). John 3:17 gives the positive form twice: God did not send the Son *ut judicet mundum, sed ut salvetur mundus*, 'so that he might judge the world, but so that the world might be saved'. The aim of the sending is what the clauses state.

The Vulgate does not always keep to this classical rule. In Matthew 7:1 the negative purpose is written *ut non judicemini*, with *ut non* where a classical author would normally put *ne*. John 18:36 does the same with *ut non traderer*. So *ut non* can introduce a purpose clause in this text.

Latin has other ways of expressing purpose, such as a relative clause with the subjunctive or *ad* with the gerundive, and the Vulgate often uses a plain infinitive instead: *misit servos suos vocare invitatos* (Matthew 22:3), 'he sent his servants to call the invited'. This lesson is about the *ut* clause.

sections.heading: Result: ut and ut non, with a signal word
body: A result clause also has *ut* with the subjunctive, but the main clause usually contains a word that points ahead to it: *ita* or *sic* ('so', 'in such a way'), *tam* ('so'), *tantus* ('so great') or *adeo* ('to such a degree'). Mark 2:2 reads *ita ut non caperet neque ad januam*, 'so that there was no longer room, not even at the door'.

The negative of a result clause is *ut non*, never *ne*. This is the classical rule, and it holds in the Vulgate. It means that *ne* is a safe sign of purpose (or of a command), while *ut non* needs a second look: it may be a negative result, or, as in Matthew 7:1, a negative purpose in Vulgate style.
A result clause states a fact that really followed (or follows). In Matthew 12:22 the man was healed *ita ut loqueretur, et videret*: he could then speak and see.

sections.heading: How to decide
body: Ask three questions in order. First, is there a signal word such as *ita* or *tantus* in the main clause? If so, expect a result clause. Second, is the negative *ne*? If so, it is a purpose clause. Third, read the sense: does the clause give an aim that someone had, or a consequence that happened?

The tense of the subjunctive follows the rules of the sequence of tenses (lesson L4.2.5), so a present subjunctive such as *judicet* goes with a main verb in a present or perfect sense, and an imperfect such as *venirent* with a past narrative. The tense helps you parse the verb. It does not tell you whether the clause is purpose or result.

Do not translate every *ut* clause with 'so that'. 'To' often serves for purpose in English ('he went to buy food'), and 'that' or 'so that' for result. Choose the English that makes the relation clear.

misunderstandings: Taking every *ut* as 'that'. With the subjunctive it begins a purpose or a result clause (and other clauses you will meet in the next lessons); with the indicative it can mean 'as' or 'when'.
Deciding purpose or result from the English 'so that' alone. English uses it for both, and you must decide from the Latin signal words and the sense.
Thinking that *ut non* always means a result clause. In the Vulgate it can also be a negative purpose, where classical Latin would have *ne*.

Reading the subjunctive as 'might' or 'may' every time. The mood marks the kind of clause. A result clause states a fact, and 'so that he could speak' or 'so that he spoke' is fairer to it than 'might'.

deeper.heading: Where the line blurs
body: Some sentences sit on the boundary between aim and outcome. John 3:16 begins with the signal word *sic*, which suggests result, yet the clause with *ut* also tells why God gave the Son. Translators and commentators differ about such verses, and the grammar alone does not settle them.

The Vulgate is a translation, and its Latin often follows its source closely. When a construction departs from the classical rules, such as *ut non* for *ne*, it is not necessarily a mistake: it shows the usage of its time and of the translator.

quoted.title: John
quoted.english: For God sent not his Son into the world, to judge the world, but that the world may be saved by him.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *judicet* is a present subjunctive, third person singular, in a purpose clause after *ut*: the aim of the sending. The second clause, *sed ut salvetur mundus*, is a second purpose clause. The main verb *misit* is a perfect that refers to the sending as an act with lasting effect, so the subjunctives are in the present.

examples.analysis: *judicemini* is a present subjunctive passive, second person plural. The clause gives the aim of the command 'do not judge': so that you may not be judged. The negative is *ut non*, not the classical *ne*.

quoted.title: Luke
quoted.english: And they beckoned to their partners that were in the other ship, that they should come and help them. And they came, and filled both the ships, so that they were almost sinking.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *adjuvarent* is an imperfect subjunctive in a purpose clause (they signalled so that the others would come and help). *mergerentur* is an imperfect subjunctive in a result clause, introduced by *ita ut*: the boats were so full that they nearly sank. One verse, two clauses of the same shape, two meanings.

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.english: Then was offered to him one possessed with a devil, blind and dumb: and he healed him, so that he spoke and saw.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *loqueretur* and *videret* are imperfect subjunctives, deponent and active, in a result clause after *ita ut*. The man was healed, and the outcome is that he spoke and saw. The clause reports what happened, not what anyone intended.

quoted.title: 1 Thessalonians
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *sit* is a present subjunctive of *sum* in a negative result clause: *ita ut non sit nobis necesse quidquam loqui*. Paul says the faith of the Thessalonians has become so well known that there is no need for him to say anything. The main verb is in the perfect, and the present subjunctive shows that the result still holds.

quoted.title: John
quoted.english: But these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God: and that believing, you may have life in his name.

options: A wish addressed to the readers
Purpose: the aim for which these things were written
Result: the writing had the consequence that they believed
practice.explain: There is no signal word such as *ita* in the main clause, and the clause says what the writing is for. That is a purpose clause: 'so that you may believe'. A result clause would have a word like *ita* or *sic* and would report what actually followed.

options: so that he went up into a boat and sat down: the crowds were so great that he did this
so that the crowds might sit
in order not to sit in a boat

check.explain: *ita ut* points to a consequence: the crowd gathered in such numbers that he got into a boat and sat down. The other renderings give a negative aim, change the subject of *sederet* or turn the clause into a condition.
